pronunciation.approximation: 'THAH-nah-tos' — aspirate the first 'th' as in 'top-hat', stress the first syllable, and keep the final 'os' short.

pronunciation.note: Thánatos is Tier 2: the Greek original carries acute stress but no long vowel. The restoration preserves the stress mark, distinguishing it from the flattened English 'Thanatos'.

domains.title: Personification of Death
domains.subtitle: The Gentle End and the Inevitable Close
domains.lead: Thánatos is the personification of death in Greek myth: not a terrifying destroyer but the quiet god who closes mortal eyes. He is the twin of Sleep, and the two are often shown together, winged youths lifting the dead from the battlefield with something like tenderness.

cards.name: Gentle Close
cards.desc: He ends life not with violence but with the touch that separates soul from body.

cards.name: Twin of Sleep
cards.desc: Hýpnos and Thánatos travel as brothers, one bringing rest, the other extinction.

cards.name: Psychopomp
cards.desc: He carries the dead from the field of honour to the house of Hades.

cards.name: Inevitable
cards.desc: Even heroes cannot bargain with him forever; death is the final common inheritance.

symbols.name: Inverted torch
symbols.meaning: Life extinguished, the flame turned downward.

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: The swiftness with which death arrives and departs.

symbols.name: Wreath
symbols.meaning: The honour due to the dead, especially warriors.

symbols.name: Butterfly or soul
symbols.meaning: The psȳché, soul, that leaves the body at death.

mythology.lead: Thánatos appears in Greek myth most often as a function rather than a character — but when he steps onto the stage, the result is unforgettable: the twin who carries heroes home, the official who keeps his appointments, and the one opponent Heracles could throw.

myths.title: The Body of Sarpedon
myths.text: When the Lycian prince Sarpedon — Zeus's own son — fell to Patroclus, the Father of Gods watched from Ida and wept: 'My heart is divided... I am caught between two griefs' (Iliad 16.435–438). He let fate take its course, then sent Apollo to lift the body, wash away the blood, anoint it with ambrosia, and wrap it in garments that ride the wind. Apollo summoned Hýpnos and Thánatos, the twin brothers, and together they lifted the hero in their arms and bore him through the air back to Lycia, where his kinsmen gave him mound and honor. It is Homer's tenderest image of death: not a terror but a carrying — the dark god as the strong son who brings the beloved body home. Even Zeus cannot abolish Thánatos; he can only ask that he be gentle.

myths.title: The Wrestler of the Tomb
myths.text: In Euripides' Alcestis (1029–1150), Admetus has won from the Fates a reprieve: another may die in his place, and his wife Alcestis has quietly volunteered. When Heracles, passing through Pherae, learns what has happened, he is ashamed before his host and resolves to act. He lies in wait at Alcestis's tomb and, as Thánatos comes with black-robed retinue to claim her, grapples with the god and throws him. 'Let go of the woman — you go below,' Heracles commands; the god, worsted, yields his prize. It is the only open defeat of Death in Greek myth, and Euripides is careful about its meaning: Thánatos is not beaten by a stronger god but by philia — by a friend's refusal to let hospitality be betrayed by grief. Death is inevitable, the play says, but for one night, love is stronger.

myths.title: Son of Night
myths.text: Hesiod makes Thánatos a child of Nyx (Night), born without a father beside his twin Hýpnos (Sleep), Kêr, and the other dark abstractions (Theogony 211–225). In the great underworld catalogue the poet describes the brothers' dwelling (756–766): there, where the bright sun never looks, Hýpnos roams peacefully over the earth and is kindly to mortals, but Thánatos has a heart of iron and a spirit pitiless as bronze; whoever he once seizes he holds fast, and he is hateful even to the deathless gods. The passage is the Greek masterpiece of unsentiment: death is not evil, not a demon to be exorcised, but a necessary power with a necessary hardness — the one office no prayer can rewrite. Hesiod's Thánatos is not cruel; he is faithful.

myths.title: The Bargain at the Door
myths.text: The Alcestis opens with its strangest scene (29–92): Thánatos arrives at Admetus's palace, drawn sword in hand, to cut the lock of hair that marks a soul for the underworld. Apollo, who owes Admetus his service, bars his way and bargains — take an older sacrifice later, take someone else. The god of death refuses, and their exchange is remarkable for its tone: Thánatos taunts Apollo, reminding him how his oracles and his son's healings have failed to save mortals, and boasts that he will take Alcestis anyway. 'An old man will come and wrestle you for her,' Apollo warns, and leaves. The scene establishes what the rest of the play proves: Thánatos knows the law exactly and yields nothing to pity, rank, or divine favor — only to force. He is, in the oldest sense, an official: incorruptible, unloved, and always on time.

lore.syncretism: Roman Mors never achieved the visual or literary richness of Greek Thánatos; Latin poets mostly kept the Greek personification. In later European art the classical winged youth slowly converged with the Grim Reaper and the Christian angel of death — the skeleton with the scythe is not Thánatos, but it inherited his inevitability. The nineteenth century gave him a strange second career: in Freud's Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920) 'Thanatos' names the death drive, twin and opponent of Eros — Greek myth converted, almost without residue, into modern psychology. The god thus became a name for the destructive forces within the self, and the word thanatology now dignifies the scholarly study of death itself.
lore.culturalLegacy: Thánatos remains one of the most resonant names for death in Western culture. He appears in psychology, philosophy, and literature whenever mortality is discussed not as an event but as a principle — the phrase 'Eros and Thanatos' still structures debates about human motivation. Hospice and grief literature repeatedly returns to the Homeric image of the winged brother lifting the fallen soldier: death not as enemy but as escort. And in the quiet personification of the gentle end — the twin of sleep rather than the horror of the grave — Greek myth preserved a dignity that later, more skeletal personifications often surrendered. His name is still invoked wherever people try to speak of death without hatred.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Thánatos is the god we do not wish to meet, yet whose presence gives life its shape. Without him, every day would be endlessly postponable; no choice would be final, no love precious because it is brief. The Greeks understood this: death is not the enemy of meaning but its frame.

His twinship with Sleep is the deeper teaching. Every night we practice death; every morning we rehearse resurrection. Thánatos is the brother who, one day, does not let us wake. To name him is to admit that the condition of being alive is being temporary — and that this is not cruelty but definition.
lore.archaeology: Thánatos received no known cult or temple in the Greek world — his existence is literary and visual. His most famous embodiment is the Euphronios krater (c. 515 BCE, Metropolitan Museum), on which Hýpnos and Thánatos, winged youths in full armor, lift the dead Sarpedon — the very scene of Iliad 16 painted within a generation of the poem's fixation. Attic white-ground lekythoi repeatedly show the pair carrying dead warriors and women, and an anonymous Athenian painter of c. 440 BCE is known to scholarship simply as the Thanatos Painter after such a scene. The Kerameikos cemetery reliefs of fallen soldiers, though unnamed, give the civic frame: a city that buried its war dead with public honor, and imagined the last journey attended.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Greek is Θάνατος, a noun meaning 'death', personified as a deity. The initial θ (theta) was an aspirated [tʰ] in Classical Greek, not the fricative [θ] of modern Greek. The acute accent falls on the first syllable. PUNICODEX writes Thánatos with the stress mark, since the spiritus asper and the full Greek letters are not registrable.
